content: The Pediatric Tuberculosis Network European Trials Group (ptbnet) conducted studies across various centers in Europe, focusing on children aged between 2 months and 15 years. The median age of participants in these studies was approximately 3 years. However, studies from India did not report specific age-related data. Mortality rates were assessed at 6 months and 12 months after treatment initiation for intervention and comparator regimens, respectively. Within six months, 6% of patients died, with most deaths occurring shortly after hospital admission and primarily involving patients diagnosed at stage 3 of the disease at baseline. Stage 3 diagnosis was strongly associated with mortality, although stage-specific outcome data were not consistently reported. Neurological sequelae were evaluated differently across studies, with 7% of patients experiencing such outcomes, most of which were categorized as mild. These sequelae were predominantly observed in patients diagnosed at stage 2 or 3. Among 135 HIV-negative and 13 HIV-positive patients in South Africa who received the intervention regimen, none experienced relapse within two years post-treatment. Other studies did not report relapse data. Due to the observational nature of the studies and the lack of comparative data, pooled proportions were reported instead of effect estimates. The certainty of evidence was deemed very low due to serious risks of bias, inconsistency, and indirectness, as well as the inability to assess imprecision. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) noted the potential benefits of the intervention regimen but highlighted the very low certainty of the evidence. They concluded that the balance of effects did not favor either the intervention or the comparator regimen. Given the rapid deterioration of children with tuberculous meningitis (TBM), the GDG refrained from favoring one regimen over the other. They also emphasized the importance of contextual factors such as acceptability, affordability, and access to child-friendly formulations, including dispersible ethionamide tablets, as well as the need for monitoring tests required for shorter regimens. The intervention regimen, which includes isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethionamide, was historically dosed using a child-friendly fixed-dose combination (FDC) of isoniazid and rifampicin (60 mg/60 mg), with pyrazinamide and ethionamide added as single medicines. However, the availability of this FDC is limited globally, while a 50/75 mg isoniazid/rifampicin dispersible tablet is widely available. Higher doses of rifampicin are being tested in ongoing trials such as SURE, TBM Kids, and OptiRif Kids, with results expected in the coming years. The GDG discussed the feasibility of introducing shorter intensive regimens, particularly in settings with high multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) burdens. They noted that the pediatric formulation of ethionamide might not be universally available. Ethionamide is a component of shorter all-oral bedaquiline-containing regimens for MDR/RR-TB, but at the time of the GDG meeting, these regimens were only recommended for children aged 6 years and above. The GDG recommended using these regimens ideally in bacteriologically confirmed drug-susceptible TBM cases, though they could also be used in clinically diagnosed cases without suspicion of drug resistance. In countries with high prevalence of drug-resistant TB, clinicians must weigh the risks and benefits of using these regimens. The current recommendation for TBM diagnosis is to use Xpert MTB/RIF or Xpert Ultra on cerebrospinal fluid as the initial diagnostic test rather than smear microscopy or culture. Monitoring and evaluation of treatment outcomes are critical to ensure high-quality implementation adapted to local contexts. Approximately 25,000–32,000 children develop MDR/RR-TB annually, with only a fraction receiving second-line treatment. Treatment outcomes for MDR-TB in children show a success rate of 78%, with higher success in clinically diagnosed cases compared to microbiologically confirmed cases. Appropriate treatment with WHO-recommended regimens is essential to ensure successful outcomes and prevent further drug resistance. Measures to prevent drug resistance include proper treatment of drug-susceptible TB, infection control, use of molecular diagnostic tests, and patient support. Bedaquiline, a novel TB drug approved in 2012, has been included in WHO recommendations for MDR-TB treatment. Initially approved for adults, its use has expanded to children aged 6–17 years in longer MDR-TB regimens. Conditional recommendations have also been made for its use in all-oral regimens for children under 6 years, though evidence remains limited. The GDG emphasized the need for continued efforts to optimize treatment options for TBM, including dosing considerations and implementation strategies.
